meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In everyone's life, at some time, our inner fire goes out. It is then burst into flame by an encounter with another human being. We should all be thankful for those people who rekindle the inner spirit'?
meta.ogDescription: Albert Schweitzer wrote the thought in his 1924 memoir. The famous wording is an anonymous paraphrase Jim Valvano printed in 1991, crediting Schweitzer.

answer.label: Not Jim Valvano — a paraphrase of Albert Schweitzer
answer.authorDates: 1875–1965 · Born in Alsace · Theologian, organist, physician and 1952 Nobel Peace Prize laureate
answer.sourceLine: Jim Valvano quoted this line twice in public, and both times he credited Albert Schweitzer — he never claimed it. The thought is genuinely Schweitzer’s, from his 1924 memoir Aus meiner Kindheit und Jugendzeit (Memoirs of Childhood and Youth), but this exact wording matches no published translation of it. Valvano’s 1991 book prints it as “a paraphrase from a speech by Albert Schweitzer” that reached him on an anonymous note.

source.heading: Where the words actually come from

docMeta.dd: Aus meiner Kindheit und Jugendzeit / Memoirs of Childhood and Youth
English by C. T. Campion, George Allen & Unwin, London, 1924 (chapter 5, p. 90)
An anonymous paraphrase; earliest instance documented by Quote Investigator is Valvano’s 1991 memoir, p. 239

source.excerpt: As a rule there are in everyone all sorts of good ideas, ready like tinder. But much of this tinder catches fire, or catches it successfully, only when it meets some flame or spark from outside, i.e. from some other person. Often, too, our own light goes out, and is rekindled by some experience we go through with a fellow-man. Thus we have each of us cause to think with deep gratitude of those who have lighted the flames within us.
trail: 1924 — Schweitzer publishes Aus meiner Kindheit und Jugendzeit; C. T. Campion’s English translation carries “Often, too, our own light goes out, and is rekindled by some experience we go through with a fellow-man.” Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section for the 1924 memoir ↗.

1955 — Erica Anderson’s The World of Albert Schweitzer: A Book of Photographs gives a different English rendering: “Sometimes our light goes out but is blown again into flame by an encounter with another human being.” Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗.
25 June 1989 — the New York Daily News prints Jim Valvano giving a version of the line and introducing it with “(Albert) Schweitzer said…”, per Quote Investigator’s citation ↗.

1991 — Valvano’s memoir prints the exact wording now in circulation, describing it as a note from an anonymous donor that paraphrased a Schweitzer speech. The book is Valvano: They Gave Me a Lifetime Contract, and Then They Declared Me Dead ↗.
source.cutTag: Memoirs of Childhood and Youth, ch. 5
source.excerptNote: This is C. T. Campion’s English translation, checked against a scan of the book. The famous three-sentence version compresses these lines and swaps in words Campion never used — “inner fire”, “encounter with another human being”, “rekindle the inner spirit”.

source.rightsNote: Two different rights questions sit on this page. Schweitzer’s memoir and Campion’s English translation were both first published in 1924, so that text — the excerpt shown above — is old enough to be public domain in the United States. The famous three-sentence wording is a different matter: nobody knows who wrote it, and its earliest documented appearance is inside an in-copyright 1991 book (Pocket Books / Simon & Schuster). Because its authorship and first publication cannot be established, we assert no status for it.

author.bio: Albert Schweitzer was a theologian, organist and musicologist who trained as a physician in middle life and founded a hospital at Lambaréné in what is now Gabon. He received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1952 for his philosophy of reverence for life. The passage behind this quotation comes from Aus meiner Kindheit und Jugendzeit (1924), the short memoir of his boyhood in Alsace, in which he argues that good ideas lie in people like tinder, waiting for a spark from someone else.

misattribution.heading: Two names on it, and neither is quite right
misattribution.intro: This line circulates under two bylines — Jim Valvano’s and Albert Schweitzer’s. The Valvano credit is simply wrong. The Schweitzer credit is right about the idea and wrong about the words.

items.why: Valvano quoted it, he did not write it. In a June 1989 Daily News column he introduced it with “(Albert) Schweitzer said…”, and in his 1991 memoir he presented it as a note from an anonymous donor that paraphrased Schweitzer. Both instances are transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. It attaches to him because his book is where the modern wording first shows up in print.

Quote sites print these three sentences as Schweitzer’s own — Goodreads gives them with no source at all ↗. The published English by C. T. Campion reads quite differently: “Often, too, our own light goes out, and is rekindled by some experience we go through with a fellow-man.” Neither “inner fire” nor “rekindle the inner spirit” is Schweitzer’s phrasing in that translation.

The anonymous note Valvano reproduced called it a paraphrase from a speech. The passage it paraphrases is written, not spoken: it comes from the memoir Aus meiner Kindheit und Jugendzeit, published in 1924, which is the source Quote Investigator traces it to ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Schweitzer wrote the thought in a book in 1924; the famous sentences are an anonymous rewrite that reached print through Jim Valvano in 1991 — with Valvano crediting Schweitzer, exactly as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

context.heading: Why the credit slides around
lead: Schweitzer’s memoir passage is an argument, not an aphorism: good ideas sit in people like unlit tinder, and it takes another person’s spark to set them going. That is hard to put on a poster. Over the decades the paragraph was compressed — first by other translators and anthologists, then by whoever wrote the note that landed on Jim Valvano’s desk — until it became three clean sentences with a thank-you at the end.

Valvano is the reason those particular sentences travel. He used a version of them in a June 1989 Daily News column while under heavy criticism at NC State, and printed the now-famous wording in his 1991 memoir. After his ESPY speech in March 1993 and his death that April, Valvano became one of the most-quoted figures in American sport — and quotations that merely appear in his book began to be re-credited to him.
context.detailsSummary: The wording drifted in three documented steps
detailsBody: 1924, C. T. Campion: “Often, too, our own light goes out, and is rekindled by some experience we go through with a fellow-man. Thus we have each of us cause to think with deep gratitude of those who have lighted the flames within us.”

1955, Erica Anderson: a looser rendering — “Sometimes our light goes out but is blown again into flame by an encounter with another human being” — which is where the phrase encounter with another human being enters English.
1991, the anonymous note in Valvano’s book: the modern three-sentence version, with “inner fire” and “rekindle the inner spirit” — wording that appears in none of the earlier translations.
